name: Bluish Purple
lede: Bluish Purple is a purple leaning toward blue, a name that began as entry 36 in Werner's nomenclature of colors and now marks a vivid screen violet.

sections.title: A purple in Werner's list
sections.body:
Werner's nomenclature, as expanded by Patrick Syme, has Bluish Purple at no. 36 among the purples [1][2]. Syme's recipe calls for about equal parts of Berlin blue and carmine red [3]. His examples are a butterfly and the purple crocus [2]. Baty's modern pairings in the same system are crocus petals and the wings of the holly blue butterfly [3].

The same mixture turns up in paint. In the fifteenth century, painters made purplish robes by glazing [[ultramarine]] with a red lake; when the lake faded, the shadows were left a deep bluish purple while the pale pink highlights remained [4]. Ball calls *The Virgin and Child before a Firescreen*, by a follower of Robert Campin around 1440, a particularly striking case of faded lake: the Virgin's robes are now almost as pale as paper, where once they were probably a warm mauve [4]. Much older recipes from Mesopotamia describe overdyeing to get both reddish and bluish purples [5].

sections.title: Two swatches, one name
sections.body:
The swatch on this page, #703BE7, comes from the xkcd color survey of 2010, and ISCC-NBS 1955 would call it a vivid violet [2]. The Werner swatch in our library is a different color altogether, a dusty blue-lavender near #8590AE [2]. The 1821 color is a quiet, aged lavender-grey, while the survey color is as saturated as a screen allows [2].

Physics blurs the names further. Violet is a spectral color, produced by very short wavelengths, while purple is a mixture of red and blue light, yet a bluish purple can look identical to violet [6]. Paterson's dictionary even defines violet as a bluish-purple color [7], and lists *cathay* as the name of a bluish purple [7].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
The vivid swatch is almost absent from painting. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, none has a color within four units of this swatch covering even one per cent of its canvas [8]. That describes this archive and these thresholds, not painting as a whole, and it is a stricter test than the five per cent used for most colors [8].

The words fared better. In Google Books, *bluish purple* peaks in the 1830s and has fallen to about 30 per cent of that peak by 2010 [9]. For purples that real painters used, see [[violet]], [[blue-violet]] and [[amethyst]]; for a painted bluish purple, look at shadows of robes in early oil painting, where ultramarine meets faded lake [4].

questions.q: What two things did Syme say make Bluish Purple?
Why did robes in some 1400s paintings end up pink with bluish-purple shadows?
choices: The red lake faded, leaving the ultramarine in the shadows
The ultramarine turned purple with age
The painters used two separate dyes
The varnish added a blue tint
questions.answer: The red lake faded, leaving the ultramarine in the shadows

questions.q: True or false: the swatch on this page is the same color as Werner's Bluish Purple.

openers: Faded red lake turned some fifteenth-century robes pink in the light and bluish purple in the folds.
Bluish Purple has two swatches a century and a half apart, and they are not the same color.
